lessons.title: Scaffolding Fundamentals for African Construction Teams
lessons.body: Scaffolding is a temporary structure that supports workers, materials, and equipment during construction, maintenance, and repair activities. In Africa, where rapid urbanisation is driving vertical growth in cities such as Lagos, Nairobi, Accra, Johannesburg, and Cairo, scaffolding competence is a core business skill. Without safe and efficient scaffolding, projects stall, injuries rise, and contractors lose money through delays and penalties. This lesson introduces the fundamentals every site supervisor, safety officer, and scaffolder must understand before erecting any structure. The first principle is that scaffolding is an engineered system, not a collection of poles and planks. Every scaffold must be designed for the loads it will carry, the height it will reach, and the environmental conditions of the site. In Africa, wind loads in coastal cities like Mombasa and Cape Town can be severe, while heat and dust in the Sahel and Kalahari regions affect worker fatigue and material durability. A scaffold that works in a temperate climate may fail in the tropics if corrosion, UV degradation of timber, and thermal expansion are ignored. The second principle is that scaffolding must be erected by competent persons under competent supervision. In many African markets, scaffolding is still assembled by general labourers without formal training. This is a business risk. A collapse can kill workers, destroy property, and expose the contractor to legal liability, reputational damage, and project shutdown. Investing in training and certification pays for itself through fewer incidents, faster erection times, and better client confidence. The third principle is load classification. Scaffolds are generally classified as light duty, medium duty, or heavy duty. Light duty scaffolds support workers and hand tools, typically up to 150 kg per bay. Medium duty scaffolds support workers and materials up to 300 kg per bay. Heavy duty scaffolds support workers and materials up to 600 kg per bay. In African projects, heavy duty scaffolds are common in concrete formwork support, block laying, and stone cladding. Misclassifying a scaffold is one of the most common causes of failure. A scaffold designed for painting should never be used to store cement bags or support a concrete skip. The fourth principle is the base. Every scaffold must stand on a firm, level, and stable foundation. In many African cities, construction sites have soft ground, un-compacted fill, or uneven surfaces. Base plates and sole boards distribute the load and prevent settlement. On sloping ground, scaffolds must be stepped or founded on a properly designed platform. Never allow a scaffold to be supported by loose bricks, blocks, or timber offcuts. The fifth principle is bracing. Scaffolds need longitudinal, transverse, and plan bracing to resist wind and lateral forces. In Africa, where open sites and high winds are common, bracing is not optional. Diagonal braces must be fixed securely to standards and ledgers using right-angle couplers or swivel couplers as appropriate. The sixth principle is access. Workers must be able to reach the working platform safely. Ladders, stair towers, or ramps must be provided and secured. In many African sites, workers climb the scaffold frame itself, which is dangerous and illegal. A properly designed access system reduces fatigue, improves productivity, and prevents falls. The seventh principle is edge protection. Guardrails, mid-rails, and toe boards must be installed on all open sides and ends of platforms. In Africa, falls from height are a leading cause of construction fatalities. Edge protection is the last line of defence and must never be omitted for speed or cost. The eighth principle is inspection and tagging. Scaffolds must be inspected before first use, after any alteration, after adverse weather, and at regular intervals. A competent person should complete a written inspection report and attach a tag indicating whether the scaffold is safe for use. In African markets, where regulatory enforcement varies, self-regulation through inspection and tagging is a competitive advantage. Clients and insurers increasingly demand documented safety systems. The ninth principle is material management. Scaffolding components must be stored, transported, and maintained properly. Steel tubes should be free of cracks, bends, and excessive corrosion. Couplers should be inspected for thread damage and deformation. Timber boards should be free of splits, knots, and rot. In humid African climates, steel rusts quickly, so painting, galvanising, or regular oiling is essential. The tenth principle is planning. Before any scaffold is erected, the team should review the drawings, identify the loads, select the system, plan the access, and sequence the work. A scaffold that is planned properly is faster to erect, safer to use, and cheaper to dismantle. In Africa, where projects often face tight deadlines and limited resources, planning is the difference between profit and loss. This lesson has introduced the core principles of scaffolding. The remaining lessons in this module will cover scaffold types, erection and dismantling procedures, inspection and maintenance, and safety management in African construction environments. By the end of this module, you will be able to plan, supervise, and inspect scaffolding operations with confidence.

lessons.title: Scaffold Types and Selection for African Projects
lessons.body: Selecting the right scaffold type is a business decision that affects cost, safety, and speed. In Africa, the most common scaffold systems are tube and coupler, modular or system scaffolds, frame scaffolds, mobile scaffolds, and suspended scaffolds. Each has advantages and limitations depending on the project. This lesson explains each type and how to choose the right one for African conditions. Tube and coupler scaffolds consist of steel tubes connected by couplers. They are flexible and can be adapted to complex shapes, which makes them popular in refurbishment, heritage buildings, and industrial plants. In Africa, tube and coupler scaffolds are widely used because they can be assembled from locally available materials and do not require proprietary components. However, they are labour-intensive, require skilled scaffolders, and are slower to erect than system scaffolds. They are also more prone to human error because every connection depends on the scaffolder tightening the coupler correctly. For projects with irregular geometry, tube and coupler is often the only practical option. Modular or system scaffolds use prefabricated frames, ledgers, and braces that lock together with wedge connections or rosettes. They are fast to erect, strong, and consistent in quality. In African cities such as Johannesburg, Lagos, and Nairobi, system scaffolds are increasingly preferred for high-rise construction, because they reduce labour costs and improve safety. The main limitation is that system scaffolds require a larger upfront investment and depend on a reliable supply chain for spare parts. Contractors should assess whether local suppliers can provide components and training before committing to a system. Frame scaffolds consist of prefabricated frames with cross-bracing and are commonly used for light to medium duty work such as painting, plastering, and maintenance. They are simple and fast to erect, but they are less flexible than tube and coupler or system scaffolds. In Africa, frame scaffolds are often used in residential and commercial building maintenance. They must be placed on firm ground and secured against overturning. Mobile scaffolds are mounted on castors or wheels, allowing them to be moved without dismantling. They are useful for indoor work, finishing, and maintenance in warehouses, airports, and shopping malls. In Africa, mobile scaffolds are common in facilities management and retail fit-outs. The key safety requirements are that the castors must be locked when the scaffold is in use, the height must not exceed three times the minimum base dimension unless outriggers are fitted, and workers must not remain on the platform while it is being moved. Suspended scaffolds are hung from overhead structures using ropes, cables, or beams. They are used for facade work, window cleaning, and bridge maintenance. In Africa, suspended scaffolds are common in high-rise cities and on bridges. They require rigorous design, redundant safety lines, and trained operators. Wind, heat, and corrosion are significant risks, so daily inspection is essential. Choosing the right scaffold type depends on several factors. The first is the work to be done. Painting a wall requires a different scaffold from supporting concrete formwork. The second is the height and duration of the work. Short-duration work at low height may suit a mobile scaffold, while long-duration work at height may require a system scaffold. The third is the load. Heavy materials such as blocks, tiles, and steel require a heavy duty scaffold. The fourth is the ground conditions. Soft or sloping ground may require a foundation design or a different scaffold type. The fifth is access. If the site is tight, a suspended scaffold may be the only option. The sixth is cost. Tube and coupler may be cheaper to buy but more expensive to erect. System scaffolds cost more upfront but save labour. The seventh is availability. In some African markets, certain systems are not available locally, which can cause delays. The eighth is regulatory requirements. Some countries have national standards for scaffolding, and some clients require specific systems. The ninth is wind and weather. Coastal and open sites require scaffolds that can resist high winds. The tenth is worker competence. A complex system scaffold is only safe if the workers are trained to erect it. In practice, most African projects use a combination of systems. A high-rise building may use system scaffolds for the main structure, tube and coupler for complex details, and mobile scaffolds for internal finishing. The key is to plan the scaffold strategy at the same time as the construction strategy, not as an afterthought. This lesson has covered the main scaffold types and selection criteria. The next lesson will cover erection and dismantling procedures, which are the highest-risk activities in scaffolding operations.

lessons.title: Erection and Dismantling Procedures for African Sites
lessons.body: Erection and dismantling are the most dangerous phases of scaffolding. In Africa, where many sites operate with tight schedules and limited supervision, these activities require strict procedures, competent workers, and clear communication. This lesson provides a practical step-by-step approach for erecting and dismantling scaffolds safely and efficiently. Before erection begins, the site must be prepared. The ground must be firm, level, and free of debris. Base plates and sole boards must be positioned according to the design. If the ground is soft, the base must be spread over a larger area using timber or concrete pads. In many African cities, construction sites are on reclaimed land, laterite, or sandy soil, so ground preparation is critical. The scaffold design must be available on site, and the scaffolders must understand it. A pre-erection briefing should cover the sequence, the loads, the access, the edge protection, and the emergency plan. The first step in erection is to set out the base. The standards, which are the vertical tubes, must be placed at the correct spacing. The ledgers, which are the horizontal tubes, must be fixed at the correct heights. The transoms, which support the platform, must be fixed at the correct spacing. In tube and coupler scaffolds, couplers must be tightened to the correct torque using a torque wrench. Over-tightening can damage the tube, and under-tightening can cause slippage. In system scaffolds, the wedge connections must be locked properly. The second step is to install bracing. Longitudinal bracing, also called face bracing, must be installed on the outer face of the scaffold. Transverse bracing, also called cross bracing, must be installed between the standards. Plan bracing must be installed at the base and at intervals to resist twisting. Bracing must be fixed to the standards and ledgers, not to the platform boards. The third step is to install the working platform. Boards must be laid tightly together, with no gaps greater than 25 mm. They must be secured against movement. In Africa, timber boards are common, but they must be of good quality and free of defects. Steel decking is increasingly used because it is stronger, lighter, and less affected by humidity. The platform must be wide enough for the work, typically at least 600 mm for light duty and 900 mm for heavy duty. The fourth step is to install edge protection. Guardrails must be at least 950 mm high, with a mid-rail at approximately 500 mm. Toe boards must be at least 150 mm high. In Africa, where falls from height are a major cause of fatalities, edge protection must be installed before the platform is used. The fifth step is to install access. Ladders must be secured and extend at least one metre above the platform. Stair towers are preferred for heights above 10 metres because they reduce fatigue and improve evacuation. Ramps must have non-slip surfaces and guardrails. The sixth step is to inspect and tag the scaffold. A competent person must check the foundation, the connections, the bracing, the platform, the edge protection, and the access. If the scaffold is safe, a tag must be attached. If it is not safe, it must be isolated and corrected. During erection, workers must use fall protection. In Africa, harnesses and lanyards are sometimes unavailable or not used. This is unacceptable. Workers must be trained to use harnesses, and the site must provide anchor points. The sequence of erection should be from the bottom up, with each lift completed before the next is started. Materials should be hoisted safely using ropes, pulleys, or mechanical hoists. Throwing materials is dangerous and must be prohibited. Dismantling is the reverse of erection, but it is often more dangerous because the scaffold is weakened as components are removed. The first step is to inspect the scaffold and plan the dismantling sequence. The second step is to clear the platform of tools and materials. The third step is to remove edge protection and access only after the platform below is ready. The fourth step is to remove the platform boards, starting from the top and working down. The fifth step is to remove bracing, ledgers, and transoms in a controlled manner. The sixth step is to remove the standards. Materials must be lowered, not dropped. In Africa, where manual labour is common, dropping materials from height is a major cause of injuries and damage. A controlled lowering system using ropes or hoists must be used. Workers must not stand on unbraced sections. During dismantling, the same fall protection rules apply. Workers must be trained, supervised, and equipped. The site must be barricaded to prevent access by other workers and the public. In many African cities, construction sites are close to public roads and markets, so barricading is essential. Communication is critical. A responsible person must be in charge of the erection and dismantling operations. Workers must be able to communicate clearly, especially when working at height. In multilingual African sites, instructions should be given in a language understood by all workers, and visual signals should be used where necessary. Weather must be monitored. Erection and dismantling should stop in high winds, heavy rain, or lightning. In Africa, sudden storms are common, especially in coastal and equatorial regions. A scaffold that is partially erected is vulnerable to wind, so it must be braced and secured at the end of each shift. This lesson has covered the key procedures for erecting and dismantling scaffolds. The next lesson will cover inspection, maintenance, and repair, which are essential for keeping scaffolds safe throughout their service life.

lessons.title: Inspection Maintenance and Repair of Scaffolding in Africa
lessons.body: Inspection, maintenance, and repair are the backbone of scaffold safety. In Africa, where scaffolding is often used intensively and stored in harsh conditions, a structured programme is essential. This lesson explains how to inspect, maintain, and repair scaffolds and their components, with practical guidance for African sites. Inspection begins with the design. Before a scaffold is erected, the design must be checked to ensure it is suitable for the intended load, height, and conditions. The design should include the foundation, the spacing of standards, the bracing, the platform, the edge protection, and the access. In Africa, where engineering resources may be limited, contractors should use standard designs or engage a qualified engineer. The first inspection is the pre-use inspection, which is carried out after erection and before the scaffold is used. A competent person must check the foundation for settlement, the base plates for contact, the standards for verticality, the ledgers and transoms for level and connection, the bracing for completeness, the platform for gaps and security, the edge protection for height and strength, and the access for safety. The inspection must be recorded in writing, and a tag must be attached to the scaffold. The tag should show the date, the inspector, the load rating, and the status. In Africa, where regulatory enforcement varies, tagging is a simple but powerful tool for safety and accountability. The second inspection is the periodic inspection, which is carried out at intervals determined by the site conditions. In general, scaffolds should be inspected at least weekly, and more often in high-risk conditions. In Africa, where heat, dust, and rain can affect materials, weekly inspection is a minimum. The third inspection is the post-event inspection, which is carried out after any event that may affect the scaffold, such as high winds, heavy rain, earth tremors, or impact from vehicles or materials. In coastal cities like Durban and Lagos, salt air accelerates corrosion, so post-storm inspections are critical. The fourth inspection is the alteration inspection, which is carried out after any modification, such as adding a lift, removing a brace, or changing the platform. Any alteration must be inspected and tagged before use. Maintenance is the routine care of scaffolding components. Steel tubes must be inspected for straightness, cracks, and corrosion. Tubes that are bent, cracked, or corroded beyond the allowable limit must be removed from service. In Africa, where storage may be outdoors, tubes should be stacked on racks off the ground and covered where possible. Couplers must be inspected for thread damage, deformation, and wear. They should be lubricated and stored in dry conditions. Timber boards must be inspected for splits, knots, rot, and insect damage. In humid African climates, termites and fungi can destroy timber quickly, so boards should be treated and stored under cover. Steel decking must be inspected for dents, cracks, and corrosion. Castors on mobile scaffolds must be inspected for free movement, locking function, and tyre condition. Ropes and cables on suspended scaffolds must be inspected for fraying, corrosion, and stretch. Repair must be carried out by competent persons using approved methods. Welding on scaffold tubes should only be done by qualified welders and should follow the manufacturer's instructions. In Africa, where counterfeit components are a risk, repairs should use genuine parts or approved equivalents. A scaffold that has been repaired must be inspected and tested before it is returned to service. Record keeping is essential. Every inspection, maintenance activity, and repair should be recorded. Records should include the date, the person, the findings, and the actions taken. In Africa, where projects may be audited by clients, insurers, or regulators, good records are a business asset. They demonstrate due diligence and can help resolve disputes. Training is the foundation of inspection and maintenance. Workers must be trained to recognise defects and report them. Supervisors must be trained to carry out inspections and keep records. In many African markets, training is available through industry associations, government agencies, and private providers. Contractors should invest in training because it reduces incidents and improves productivity. Common defects to look for include bent standards, loose couplers, missing braces, cracked boards, missing toe boards, damaged guardrails, and blocked access. In Africa, where scaffolds are sometimes used by multiple trades, defects can be caused by misuse. For example, a scaffold may be used to support a hoist or to store materials beyond its load rating. Supervisors must control access and use. Environmental factors must be considered. In hot climates, steel can expand and cause connections to loosen. In dusty environments, couplers can seize. In rainy seasons, foundations can soften and settle. In coastal areas, salt spray can accelerate corrosion. A maintenance programme should be adjusted to the local environment. This lesson has covered inspection, maintenance, and repair. The final lesson will cover safety management, legal requirements, and business practices for scaffolding in Africa.

lessons.title: Safety Management and Business Practices for Scaffolding in Africa
lessons.body: Safety management is not just a legal obligation; it is a business strategy. In Africa, where construction is growing rapidly and competition is intense, contractors that manage scaffolding safety well win more work, retain better workers, and reduce costs. This lesson covers safety management systems, legal requirements, worker training, and business practices for scaffolding operations in African markets. A safety management system for scaffolding should include a policy, planning, implementation, monitoring, and review. The policy should state the company's commitment to safe scaffolding and define responsibilities. Planning should identify the risks, the controls, and the resources needed. Implementation should include training, supervision, inspection, and maintenance. Monitoring should include audits, incident reporting, and performance indicators. Review should include lessons learned and continuous improvement. In Africa, where formal systems may be less common, a simple but effective system is better than a complex system that is not used. Risk assessment is the core of safety management. For scaffolding, the main risks are falls from height, falling objects, scaffold collapse, electrocution, and manual handling injuries. In Africa, falls from height are the leading cause of construction fatalities. Controls should follow the hierarchy of elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment. For example, eliminate the need to work at height by using ground-level assembly. Substitute a safer scaffold type. Engineer controls such as guardrails and toe boards. Administer controls such as permits and training. Use personal protective equipment such as harnesses and helmets as a last line of defence. Legal requirements vary across Africa. Some countries have comprehensive occupational health and safety laws, while others have limited enforcement. In South Africa, the Occupational Health and Safety Act and the Construction Regulations set specific requirements for scaffolding. In Kenya, the Occupational Safety and Health Act applies. In Nigeria, the Factories Act and the Labour Act apply. In Ghana, the Labour Act and the Factories, Offices and Shops Act apply. Contractors must know the law in each country where they operate. Even where enforcement is weak, clients and insurers may impose their own requirements. Worker training is essential. Scaffolders should be trained in the type of scaffold they erect, the loads, the bracing, the access, the edge protection, and the inspection. Supervisors should be trained in planning, supervision, and inspection. In Africa, training should be practical and delivered in local languages where possible. Workers should be assessed and certified. Refresher training should be provided regularly. Supervision is the link between training and safe practice. A competent supervisor must be present during erection, dismantling, and alteration. The supervisor must ensure that the design is followed, that workers use fall protection, that the scaffold is inspected and tagged, and that unsafe conditions are corrected. In Africa, where labour is often casual, supervision must be clear and consistent. Communication should be in a language understood by all workers. Personal protective equipment must be provided and used. This includes helmets, safety boots, gloves, high-visibility clothing, and harnesses. In Africa, where heat is a factor, workers should be encouraged to drink water and take breaks. Heat stress can cause mistakes and injuries. Emergency planning is essential. The site should have a rescue plan for workers who fall or become trapped. In Africa, where emergency services may be far away or unreliable, the site should have trained first aiders and rescue equipment. The plan should be practised. Incident reporting and investigation are important. Every incident, including near misses, should be reported and investigated. The investigation should identify the causes and the actions needed to prevent recurrence. In Africa, where under-reporting is common, contractors should create a culture where workers feel safe to report. Business practices for scaffolding include pricing, contracts, and cash flow. Scaffolding is often a significant cost on a project. Contractors should price scaffolding based on the design, the duration, the labour, the materials, and the risk. Under-pricing leads to corner-cutting and unsafe practices. Contracts should clearly define the scope, the responsibilities, the payment terms, and the safety requirements. In Africa, where payment delays are common, contractors should manage cash flow carefully. They should avoid buying cheap, substandard components that fail early. They should invest in good quality scaffolds and maintain them well. They should train their workers and keep records. They should build relationships with clients, suppliers, and regulators. They should learn from incidents and improve. They should benchmark their performance against industry best practice. Technology can help. Mobile apps can be used for inspection checklists and reporting. GPS can be used to track equipment. Drones can be used to inspect tall scaffolds. In Africa, where mobile phone penetration is high, simple digital tools can improve safety and efficiency. Finally, safety is a competitive advantage. Clients increasingly require safe scaffolding. Insurers offer lower premiums to contractors with good safety records. Workers prefer to work for contractors who care about their safety. A strong safety culture attracts talent, reduces turnover, and improves productivity. This module has covered the fundamentals, types, erection and dismantling, inspection and maintenance, and safety management of scaffolding. By applying these lessons, you can build a scaffolding operation that is safe, efficient, and profitable in any African market.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Scaffolding Materials, Load Tables and Site Records for African Projects

This module is the working reference sheet for supervisors, quantity surveyors and business owners who price, procure and hand over scaffolding in African markets. It sits after Module 4 (Inspection, Maintenance and Repair) and Module 5 (Safety Management and Business Practices), and it exists for one reason: most scaffolding losses on African sites are not caused by bad erectors. They are caused by undocumented material substitution, unverified tube thickness, and missing handover records that turn a profitable hire contract into an uninsured liability.

Use this lesson at the point of procurement and at the point of handover. Print the checklist, keep the load table on site, and attach the inspection record to every invoice. In markets where imported tube is re-rolled locally, where second-hand couplers circulate between projects, and where a single rain season can destroy a storage yard, the paper trail is the margin.

â  SAFETY WARNING â HEALTH AND CHEMICAL EXPOSURE

Scaffolding work in Africa frequently involves galvanised tube, paint, solvents, cutting oils and cement dust. These are hazardous substances. The following are non-negotiable:

  • Galvanised tube cutting and welding releases zinc oxide fume. Weld only in ventilated areas, wear a P2/P3 respirator, and never weld inside a closed storage container.
  • Solvents and paints used to mark or protect tube can cause dermatitis and respiratory irritation. Use nitrile gloves, eye protection and skin barrier cream.
  • Cement dust from adjacent formwork is a respiratory sensitiser. Enforce dust masks and water suppression within the scaffold footprint.
  • Do not eat, drink or smoke on the scaffold. Wash hands before breaks.
  • Keep a written COSHH-equivalent register for every chemical on site, with the safety data sheet in the site office.

Source: WHO, Preventing Disease Through Healthy Environments: Occupational Risks (Geneva: WHO, 2021); and MSD Animal Health / MSD occupational health guidance on chemical handling in field operations (2022).

Quick Reference Checklist â on-site material and handover control

  1. Verify tube wall thickness on delivery. Sample at least 10% of each batch with a caliper or ultrasonic gauge. Reject anything below 3.0 mm for hire-grade tube.
  2. Check coupler provenance. Drop-forged couplers carry a manufacturer mark and a batch number. Reject unmarked or cracked couplers â they are the most common cause of scaffold collapse in the region.
  3. Grade boards before erection. Reject boards with splits, knots larger than one-third of the width, or evidence of fungal decay after the rain season.
  4. Log every batch. Record supplier, date, batch number, inspector name and result in a site register. This is your evidence in a claim.
  5. Store under cover. Tube stored on bare ground in high-rainfall zones corrodes within one season. Use timber dunnage and tarpaulins.
  6. Issue a handover certificate. Every completed scaffold must be signed off by a competent inspector before use, with a tag fixed at the access point.
  7. Price the paper trail. Include inspection, tagging and record-keeping in your quotation. Clients who refuse to pay for it are the clients who generate claims.
  8. Review after every rain season. Re-inspect all hire stock for corrosion, bent tube and coupler slip before it goes to the next site.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Code of Practice for the Safe Use of Construction Materials in Small and Medium Enterprises (free PDF, Rome, 2019).
  • WHO â Preventing Disease Through Healthy Environments: Occupational Risks (free, Geneva, 2021).
  • UK HSE â Scaffolding Technical Guidance (HSG150) (free guidance, applicable to EN-standard tube and couplers used across Africa).
  • ILRI â Market and Employment Data for Construction Services in East Africa (free, Nairobi, 2023).
  • ILO â Safety and Health in Construction (free code of practice, Geneva).

Business note. The scaffolding business in Africa is a records business. The contractor who can produce a batch register, a coupler test log and a signed handover certificate wins the tender, survives the audit and gets paid. The one who cannot, absorbs the loss. Price the paperwork, keep the paperwork, and the margin follows.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a base plate on a scaffold?
options: A) To connect guardrails to the frame
B) To distribute the load over a larger area
C) To anchor the scaffold to a building
D) To support the scaffold planks
quiz.explanation: Base plates spread the scaffold load over a wider area to prevent sinking into the ground.

quiz.q: Which component is used to join two scaffold tubes at right angles?
options: A) Swivel coupler
B) Base collar
C) Right angle coupler
D) Putlog
quiz.explanation: A right angle coupler, also called a fixed coupler, joins tubes at 90 degrees.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended height for a freestanding mobile scaffold?
options: A) Twice the minimum base dimension
B) Three times the minimum base dimension
C) Four times the minimum base dimension
D) Five times the minimum base dimension
quiz.explanation: Freestanding mobile scaffolds should not exceed three times the minimum base dimension unless outriggers are used.

quiz.q: What does the term putlog refer to in scaffolding?
options: A) A vertical load bearing member
B) A diagonal brace for stability
C) A tie that anchors to a wall
D) A horizontal member that supports the platform and sits in a brick hole
quiz.explanation: A putlog is a horizontal member, often used in putlog scaffolds, that rests in holes in the wall to support the platform.

quiz.q: Before using a scaffold, what should a user check first?
options: A) That a valid scafftag or inspection tag is in place
B) That the scaffold is painted a bright color
C) That the scaffold has been in use for at least a week
D) That the scaffold is made of steel only
quiz.explanation: A valid scafftag or inspection tag confirms the scaffold has been inspected and is safe to use.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common cause of scaffold collapse?
options: A) Using too many guardrails
B) Overloading the platform beyond its rated capacity
C) Installing toe boards
D) Using base plates on firm ground
quiz.explanation: Overloading the platform beyond its rated capacity is a leading cause of scaffold failure.

quiz.q: What is the minimum height for a top guardrail on a scaffold?
options: A) 500 mm
B) 750 mm
C) 950 mm
quiz.explanation: The top guardrail should be at least 950 mm above the platform, with an intermediate rail at about 470 mm.

quiz.q: When must a scaffold be inspected by a competent person?
options: A) Only after a serious incident
B) Once every month regardless of use
C) Only when first erected
